findings.text: The virtual IOAPIC offers operations to capture and restore its state. Capture copies the device image to caller storage while filtering delivered remote indications from the pending word. Restore copies caller storage into the device, clears both pending words, requests a rescan of the table, and replays the caller pending word through the injection path. Both operations serialize against concurrent activity with the device lock.

Virtual IOAPIC state combines addressing and selection registers, identity and pending words, a per pin redirection table, per pin level tracking, an embedded generic IO device, a back reference to the owning virtual machine, a serializing lock, RTC end of interrupt tracking with delayed work and per pin counters, a delivered marker, and a mask notifier chain whose readers and writers use different synchronization.

Each redirection entry can be viewed as a single 64 bit quantity or as decoded controls for vector, delivery style, destination style, delivery status, polarity, remote state, trigger style, mask state, reserved space and destination target.

RTC tracking records whether an end of interrupt is outstanding, which virtual CPUs already received the notification, and which vector each such CPU received, with vectors meaningful only where the bitmap indicates delivery.
Mask notification entries link into the IOAPIC chain and carry the affected line number plus a callback that runs when masking changes.

Pin count aliases the generic KVM pin count. Reported version is 0x11. Edge encoding is 0 and level encoding is 1. Default base is 0xfec00000 with span 0x100. Selector is at offset 0x00 and data window at 0x10. Direct registers are identifier at 0x00, version at 0x01 and arbitration at 0x02, with identifier and arbitration noted as x86 only.
Delivery styles are fixed 0, lowest priority 1, PMI 2, NMI 4, INIT 5 and external 7. The real time clock is wired to line 8.

Whether a virtual CPU has pending timer activity aggregates two subsystems. The local APIC contributes only when in kernel, and only when the unit is enabled and its timer entry is unmasked as judged by the masked bit. The Xen subsystem contributes only when its timer is enabled, with a disabled build always reporting none and an enabled build additionally requiring hypercall enablement and a positive pending counter.

A CPU is considered to have an injectable interrupt when an external interrupt is pending. Otherwise, when not in nested guest mode but with active virtualized APIC state, no local APIC interrupt is reported. In remaining cases local APIC pending state decides.

External interrupt fetch reports absence when none is pending. Without an in kernel local APIC it returns the stored interrupt number. With it, Xen upcall takes precedence when Xen reports an interrupt, then the programmable controller value when that controller is in kernel, otherwise the split irqchip userspace pending vector is consumed and cleared to the absent marker.

Overall interrupt fetch prefers the external source and returns it immediately when present. Only when external is absent does it consult the local APIC, and a delivered local APIC vector is acknowledged as part of the fetch.

Acknowledge validates its inputs and ignores missing state with a one time warning. It always clears the request bit. Auto end of interrupt vectors then refresh priority state to allow a further higher priority pending vector to raise an event. Normal vectors set the in service bit and update priority under the assumption that no higher pending vector exists absent concurrent injection. Request clearing and service setting maintain software caches for pending state, service count and highest service only without hardware virtualization; with virtualization they update hardware register state and notify hardware, ignoring duplicate service sets.

Pending timer injection fans out to the local APIC injector when that subsystem is in kernel and to the Xen injector when the Xen timer is enabled, with a disabled Xen build providing an empty operation. Timer migration moves local APIC state plus the programmable timer when IOAPIC support is present plus vendor specific state.

Local APIC timer migration does nothing when the APIC is not in kernel or when posted interrupts can deliver directly. Otherwise it attempts to cancel the high resolution timer and rearms it at its existing expiry only when cancellation found it still queued.

Local APIC injection checks its pending counter and only when positive delivers through the APIC path and resets the counter. Xen injection similarly checks its pending counter and only when positive signals a two level event on the timer port of the same CPU, then clears expiry and pending state.

Fast event signaling resolves its target by cached index when nonnegative else by identifier lookup and caches the result, rejecting unknown CPUs and out of range ports. Under shared protection it validates the shared area and selects native or compat layout from long mode. Setting the pending bit yields already set, masked with poller consideration, or newly delivered. New delivery updates the guest selector word and upcall flag when guest memory is accessible, else records in a kernel shadow and requests a kick. When a per CPU lapic vector is configured the kick is replaced by immediate vector injection.

The sleeping event path first attempts fast delivery and returns unless a retry is requested. When the caller lacks the virtual machine address space it borrows that space, rejecting callers that already hold an unexpected space. It then repeatedly retries fast delivery and refreshes the shared info cache under sleepable protection until delivery succeeds or fails with a terminal status, finally releasing any borrowed space.

Channel capacity depends on address width and long mode, with distinct native and compat limits. A polling CPU is only woken when it polls the signaled port or polls generically and its poll mask bit transitions from set to clear, in which case an unblock request and kick are issued.

Lookup by identifier rejects negative values, succeeds immediately when the same numeric index holds a matching identifier, otherwise scans all CPUs for a matching identifier and reports absence when none matches.

Interrupt file descriptor permission depends on irqchip completeness: resample requests need a full irqchip while plain requests need any in kernel irqchip. Both the irqchip presence query and the routing permission query delegate to the in kernel irqchip test.

Message signaled interrupts are decoded from routing entry address and data into destination, vector, destination style, trigger style derived from level encoding, delivery style and redirection hint, with level asserted and no destination shorthand. Routes are invalid when extended APIC format is active and high address bits are set. Injection rejects invalid routes and deasserted levels, otherwise delivers the decoded interrupt to the local APIC subsystem.

Atomic interrupt setting handles synthetic HyperV interrupts, message signaled interrupts through a fast local APIC attempt, and Xen events through fast event signaling with deasserted levels ignored. All other routing types report a retry status so the caller can use sleeping context.

The IRQ line control requires an in kernel irqchip, forwards the requested line and level through the core setter with a userspace source identifier, and returns the resulting line status to the caller.

Routing setup validates by type. Programmable controller entries are rejected for split irqchip, enforce per controller pin ranges with slave pins biased, and bind to the matching controller setter. Message signaled entries bind to the MSI setter with address validation. Synthetic entries record CPU and index. Xen entries delegate to Xen setup. Unknown types are rejected. Callers initializing the irqchip may invoke this before the irqchip is marked in kernel, so other callers must check routability first.

Xen routing setup accepts only two level priority. It records port, CPU identifier and priority with the event setter, resolves the CPU index at setup when the CPU exists and records unknown otherwise to tolerate restore before CPU creation, and intentionally skips port range checks so routing can be restored independently of the long mode flag that changes capacity.
Snapshot capture and restore serialize the entire copy plus pending state adjustment and replay under the virtual IOAPIC spin lock.

Fast event delivery holds sleepable protection across the whole operation and holds the cache lock with interrupts saved while validating and updating shared and per CPU areas, releasing and reacquiring when switching from shared to per CPU caches.
The mask notifier chain uses sleepable read side protection for traversal and a separate IRQ lock for mutation.

Restoring IOAPIC state discards all prior pending and delivered markers before replaying caller state, so concurrent level changes outside the locked window can be lost. Acknowledging with an invalid vector or without a local APIC must leave request and service state untouched. Message signaled routes that violate extended format addressing must be rejected rather than delivered.

Event delivery distinguishes already set, masked and newly delivered outcomes and a retry outcome that requires cache refresh in sleeping context; treating retry as success would drop the event. Borrowing virtual machine memory when the caller already runs with unrelated memory is rejected. Poller wakeups must only fire on matching port conditions to avoid spurious unblocks.

Timer pending counters are only acted upon when positive and are reset after the corresponding injection, with Xen also clearing its expiry. The userspace external pending holder returns its stored vector once and resets to the absent marker.
The IOAPIC header uses an include guard and the IRQ implementation prefixes diagnostics with its module name.
